newsitem.title: UK: Bank of Scotland chief warns on sales tax.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Scotland chief warns on sales tax.

text.p: Bank of Scotland governor Sir Bruce Pattullo has warned against a regional sales tax in Scotland which might come as a result of a planned devolution of political power.
Writing in the bank's annual report, published on Thursday, Pattullo said such a tax would handicap business and discourage investment not only in Scotland but elsewhere in Britain.
Britain's new Labour Party government is committed to holding a referendum where Scots will be asked to endorse their own elected assembly and whether or not it should have tax-raising powers.

"Many uncertainties remain to be resolved," Pattullo wrote. "The proposal of fiscal powers to vary the basic rate income tax by up to 3p in the pound is controversial and, in our view, many serious collection, administrative and motivational problems remain hidden."

"Any form of additional regional tax can only handicap Scottish business and commerce and discourage vital investment in the UK and overseas companies - and thus the all important creation of wealth and jobs," he adds.
Pattullo said the entire Scottish electorate would have to think very seriously about this risk and any adverse consequences flowing from such a tax over the longer term.

He added that he did not wish to influence the electorate in any way by his views and , despite his downbeat message, Sir Bruce claimed that Bank of Scotland had successfully lived with many changes in its 300-year history.
"I am confident it has the ability once again to adapt its structure and procedures in whatever way may be required."
Turning to another constitutional issue, Pattullo again aired his deep concerns over Britain's potential membership of European monetary union (EMU).

He says that any country which joined without meeting the substance of the convergence criteria and without its political leaders fully explaining the degree by which economic sovereignty must be permanently ceded to a European central bank - "was taking a very grave risk."
In the absence of any exit mechanism, subsequent disillusion in any nation state would inevitably lead to a resurgence of nationalism, "leading in turn to social and political unrest."
In a radio interview, devolution minister Henry McLeish disputed Pattullo's line. He said plans for tax varying powers were based solely on income tax.

The tax raising issue caused some controversy in Britain's recent election campaign when Labour promised not to raise the basic rate of income tax in Britain during the life of the parliament, thus seeming to immediately restrict the powers of any Scottish assembly.
